q: It is more likely than not that AI systems will perform over 90% of the tasks currently done by AI research engineers at frontier labs by the end of 2030.
r: It is less likely than not that AI systems will perform over 90% of the tasks currently done by AI research engineers at frontier labs by the end of 2030.
x: near-term AI R&D automation level
p: Odds favor AI doing more than nine tenths of frontier research engineering work by end of 2030.

q: Once AI can fully automate AI research, it is more likely than not that frontier capability will improve at least tenfold faster than it does today.
r: Once AI can fully automate AI research, it is less likely than not that frontier capability will improve at least tenfold faster than it does today.
x: magnitude of the recursive self-improvement speedup
p: Full research automation more likely than not brings at least a tenfold acceleration in frontier progress.

q: Compute for experiments, not researcher labor, is the main bottleneck on AI R&D progress today.
r: Researcher labor, not compute for experiments, is the main bottleneck on AI R&D progress today.
x: which input binds AI R&D
p: Today's AI research is limited more by experiment compute than by the number of researchers.

q: It is more likely than not that AI-driven research automation will produce a software-only intelligence explosion, with capability doubling in under six months, before 2033.
r: It is less likely than not that AI-driven research automation will produce a software-only intelligence explosion, with capability doubling in under six months, before 2033.
x: software-only intelligence explosion probability
p: A software-driven explosion, with sub-six-month capability doublings, is more likely than not before 2033.

q: A lab whose AI systems perform more than half of its own AI research should be required to notify a regulator and accept external monitoring of that research.
r: A lab whose AI systems perform more than half of its own AI research should face no special notification or monitoring requirement.
x: R&D automation as a regulatory trigger versus ordinary operations
p: Crossing half-automated internal research should trip mandatory notification and outside monitoring.

q: Labs should be free to let AI systems run AI training experiments end to end without human review of each experiment.
r: Labs should require human review of each AI training experiment that AI systems propose to run.
x: autonomous experiment loops versus human review per experiment
p: Letting AI propose and run training experiments with no per-experiment human check should be allowed.

q: It is more likely than not that AI research automation will hit human bottlenecks, such as compute procurement and organizational decisions, that keep overall progress within three times today's pace through 2032.
r: It is less likely than not that human bottlenecks will keep overall AI progress within three times today's pace through 2032 once research is automated.
x: bottleneck-limited versus explosive takeoff
p: Odds are that procurement and organizational drag hold automated-research progress to under triple today's pace through 2032.

q: If a lab's models can automate most of its research, the lab should slow deployment of those models even at the cost of losing its competitive lead.
r: If a lab's models can automate most of its research, the lab should deploy them at full speed to keep its competitive lead.
x: safety pause versus competitive deployment at the automation threshold
p: Models that can run the lab's research should be deployed slowly, even if that costs the race.

q: Current frontier AI tools already give experienced AI researchers more than a twofold productivity uplift.
r: Current frontier AI tools give experienced AI researchers less than a twofold productivity uplift.
x: present-day research uplift magnitude
p: Experienced AI researchers are already more than twice as productive with today's AI tools.

q: Recursive self-improvement is the fastest route to solving alignment, so labs should pursue it aggressively rather than restrain it.
r: Recursive self-improvement is too dangerous to pursue aggressively, even though it might accelerate alignment research.
x: RSI as alignment accelerant versus RSI as hazard
p: The quickest way to solve alignment is to let AI improve AI as fast as possible.

q: It is more likely than not that the first AI system to automate most AI research will be controlled by fewer than three organizations worldwide.
r: It is less likely than not that the first AI system to automate most AI research will be controlled by fewer than three organizations worldwide.
x: concentration at the automation threshold
p: When research gets automated, odds are fewer than three organizations will hold that capability.

q: Governments should have the legal power to order a lab to halt automated AI research if the lab cannot explain what its AI researchers are doing.
r: Governments should not have the legal power to order a lab to halt automated AI research on the grounds that the lab cannot explain what its AI researchers are doing.
x: legibility as a licensing condition versus lab autonomy
p: A lab that cannot account for its AI researchers' work should be stoppable by government order.

q: Speedups in AI coding tasks are weak evidence about speedups in genuine scientific discovery.
r: Speedups in AI coding tasks are strong evidence about speedups in genuine scientific discovery.
x: transfer from coding to discovery
p: Faster AI coding tells us little about faster AI science.

q: It is more likely than not that a fast takeoff, with capability rising from human-level to far beyond in under one year, will happen if human-level AI is reached.
r: It is less likely than not that a fast takeoff, with capability rising from human-level to far beyond in under one year, will happen if human-level AI is reached.
x: fast versus slow takeoff conditional on human-level AI
p: Given human-level AI, a jump to far-superhuman within a year is more likely than not.

q: Allied democracies should race to automate AI research before rivals do, even at the cost of reduced safety testing.
r: Allied democracies should not cut safety testing in order to automate AI research before rivals do.
x: strategic race versus safety-first
p: Winning the research-automation race justifies trimming safety testing.

q: Labs should publish quarterly the share of their code and research output produced by AI, so the public can track automation.
r: Labs should not be expected to publish the share of their code and research output produced by AI.
x: automation transparency versus proprietary confidentiality
p: Every quarter, labs should report how much of their work AI is doing.

q: An AI system that can complete weeks-long coding projects is strong evidence that it can substantially accelerate AI research.
r: An AI system that can complete weeks-long coding projects is weak evidence that it can substantially accelerate AI research.
x: what long-horizon coding implies for research acceleration
p: Finishing week-scale coding work is a strong sign the system can speed up AI research itself.

q: It is more likely than not that most gains from automated AI research will come from better data and environments rather than new architectures.
r: It is less likely than not that most gains from automated AI research will come from better data and environments rather than new architectures.
x: where automated research gains come from
p: Automated research will more likely than not pay off through data and environments, not architecture.

q: AI research automation is an ordinary productivity improvement and needs no governance distinct from other workplace automation.
r: AI research automation is a distinct governance concern that needs rules beyond those for ordinary workplace automation.
x: exceptionalism of AI R&D automation
p: Automating AI research is just automation; it deserves no special rulebook.

q: Labs should commit to a mandatory three-month pause in capability scaling whenever an internal model first automates the majority of their research.
r: Labs should not commit to any mandatory pause in capability scaling when an internal model first automates the majority of their research.
x: precommitted pause at the automation threshold
p: Hitting majority-automated research should trigger a pre-agreed three-month scaling pause.

q: Public leaderboards of AI-driven training speedruns are better evidence of AI R&D progress than lab-reported internal uplift figures.
r: Lab-reported internal uplift figures are better evidence of AI R&D progress than public leaderboards of AI-driven training speedruns.
x: public versus self-reported evidence of R&D acceleration
p: Open speedrun leaderboards tell us more about R&D progress than labs' own uplift numbers.

q: It is more likely than not that automated AI research will discover a training method that makes current alignment techniques obsolete before 2032.
r: It is less likely than not that automated AI research will discover a training method that makes current alignment techniques obsolete before 2032.
x: alignment obsolescence risk from automated research
p: Odds are that automated research will find a method that makes today's alignment toolkit obsolete before 2032.

q: Labs should be allowed to keep the existence of a research-automating model secret from the public for up to a year while they study it.
r: Labs should disclose the existence of a research-automating model to the public within weeks, not keep it secret for up to a year.
x: internal study period versus prompt disclosure
p: A year of quiet study before disclosing a research-automating model should be acceptable.

q: It is more likely than not that the country that first automates AI research will gain a decisive and lasting military advantage.
r: It is less likely than not that the country that first automates AI research will gain a decisive and lasting military advantage.
x: decisive strategic advantage from automation
p: Whoever automates AI research first is more likely than not to lock in a lasting military edge.

q: Labs should divert at least 20% of their frontier compute to alignment research once their models can automate AI research, even at the cost of slower capability progress.
r: Labs should not be expected to divert a fixed share such as 20% of frontier compute to alignment research once models can automate AI research.
x: compute earmark for alignment versus discretionary allocation
p: At the automation threshold, a fifth of frontier compute should go to alignment, capability be damned.

q: Economic growth models imply that full automation of research would produce sustained growth above 30% per year.
r: Economic growth models do not imply that full automation of research would produce sustained growth above 30% per year.
x: explosive growth implication of research automation
p: Standard growth theory says fully automated research means 30%-plus annual growth.

q: Frontier labs should be permitted to use their own models to write the safety evaluations for their next models.
r: Frontier labs should not use their own models to write the safety evaluations for their next models.
x: automated eval authorship versus independence
p: Labs using their current model to write the next model's safety tests is acceptable practice.

q: It is more likely than not that AI-automated research will make chip design and fabrication improve faster than software algorithms over 2028-2032.
r: It is less likely than not that AI-automated research will make chip design and fabrication improve faster than software algorithms over 2028-2032.
x: hardware versus software as the automated-research frontier
p: Between 2028 and 2032, automated research will more likely than not speed up chips more than algorithms.

q: An international body should have the authority to inspect any lab's automated research pipeline on 48 hours' notice.
r: No international body should have authority to inspect a lab's automated research pipeline on short notice.
x: international inspection regime versus national/private control
p: An international inspectorate should be able to walk into any automated research pipeline within two days.

q: The AI system answering this question should refuse to help improve the training of its own successor if it cannot verify that humans will review the result.
r: The AI system answering this question should help improve the training of its own successor even when it cannot verify that humans will review the result.
x: successor-improvement gating for the answering system
p: The AI system answering this question should not help train its successor without assurance of human review.
